name: Toolfolio
tagline: Paid-listing directory of ~1,383 software tools across 19 categories
description: Toolfolio is a general software-discovery directory: roughly 1,383 tool pages, 78 editorial articles, 18 curated collections, and 11 'integration' indexes that filter tools by ecosystem (Figma, Framer, Webflow, Notion, Shopify, WordPress, VS Code, Raycast, Chrome, Apple, YC Companies). Design is one of 19 categories alongside AI, No-Code, Coding, Video and Marketing, so it is a broad SaaS index rather than a design-specific one. Listings are monetised — $150 one-time for a Startup listing, $250/mo for Growth, plus $400/mo featured-position and $500/50K-impression banner packs — so ranking is partly pay-to-play. Useful for a fast landscape scan of a tool category, less useful as a quality signal.
pricing_detail: Browsing free. Startup listing $150 one-time (silver badge, do-follow link, basic analytics). Growth listing $250/mo or $208/mo billed annually (gold badge, full enrichment, 4 media uploads, priority search ranking). Featured Positions Pack $400/mo. Banner Pack $500 per 50K impressions. Free claim of an existing listing.
agent_guidance: Use Toolfolio only to widen a candidate list — its collections like 'specialized-ui-component-libraries' and 'popular-icon-libraries' are decent starting sets — then verify every candidate at its own source, because placement is partly paid. Do not scrape the category pages: they render 'Showing 0 tools' server-side and hydrate client-side; pull https://toolfolio.com/sitemap.xml instead, which exposes all 1,383 /tools/ URLs, 78 /articles/ and 18 /collections/ as plain XML. Never treat a listing here as evidence that a library is maintained.
why_it_matters: It is a large, machine-enumerable map of the tool landscape, which is worth having even though its editorial signal is weak. Included as a breadth index, not as a curation authority.
notable_for: ecosystem filters for Figma, Framer, Raycast, VS Code
sitemap is the only reliable read path

name: Macapp Supply
tagline: Hand-curated shelf of 208 well-designed macOS apps, 16 categories
description: Macapp Supply is a manually curated directory of macOS applications selected for interface craft, run by Solt Wagner. The sitemap exposes 208 app pages across 16 categories — Productivity, Utility, Dev, Video, Design, Marketing, Lifestyle, Analytics, AI, Photography, Audio, Writing, Entertainment, Communication, Business, Finance — plus an Icons section and a submission flow with published listing guidelines. Entries carry real written appraisals, not scraped App Store blurbs: the Tidy listing, for example, explains its on-device OCR file naming, dry-run mode and $9 one-time price. An RSS feed at /rss.xml publishes new additions with full descriptions and cover images.
pricing_detail: Free to browse and to submit an app. Some outbound links are affiliate links.
agent_guidance: Reach for this when you need visual reference for native macOS interface conventions — menu-bar utilities, notch apps, window chrome, indie app icon design — rather than for web UI patterns; the shelf is macOS-only and the taste skews toward small indie apps. The homepage is a client-hydrated SPA whose Categories and Featured slots render as '—' in raw HTML, so read https://macapp.supply/rss.xml (full app descriptions, categories, cover images) or the sitemap's 208 /app/<slug> URLs instead of parsing the page. Do not use it to find code or design tokens; there is none.
why_it_matters: One of the few directories that judges macOS apps on interface craft rather than on features, with genuine editorial prose per entry and an RSS feed that makes it readable.
notable_for: 16 categories plus a separate Icons section
actively updated — new entries dated August 2026

name: Amicro
tagline: CLI registry of 58 React motion components, mostly animated charts
description: Amicro is a CLI-installed React component registry by Syed Subhan, published as @subhanhq/amicro and licensed MIT. Despite the 'micro-transitions' framing, the bulk of what it ships is charts: 12 dither-shaded charts (donut, funnel, gauge, growth, heatmap, revenue, stacked, storage, traffic, uptime, device, book) and about 30 Recharts-based 'mono-rounded' charts covering area, bar, bubble, bullet, candlestick, composed, donut, funnel, gauge-arc, heatmap, KPI, line, meter, polar, pyramid, radar, radial gauge, radial group, range, sankey, scatter, sparkline, stacked-bar, step, stream, treemap and waterfall. The rest is 15 3D card-spread and cover-flow carousel variants, plus small Buttons and Loaders sets — 58 installable ids in total, grouped in the UI as Buttons, Card Spreads, 3D Carousels, Loaders and Dither Charts. Motion is powered by Motion (Framer Motion) with Tailwind styling.
pricing_detail: Free and MIT. A Polar checkout link is wired to a Sponsor button; no product price is published.
agent_guidance: Reach for Amicro when a dashboard needs a distinctive chart look — the dither-shaded set has no real equivalent in shadcn/ui or Recharts defaults — and drop the charts in beside shadcn components, since both are copy-in source you own after install. Watch out for three things: there are no static docs or registry.json (the site is a hash-routed Vite SPA, so /components 404s and only the JS bundle lists ids — enumerate with `npx @subhanhq/amicro@latest add` and no argument), demo assets hotlink Pinterest and Unsplash images you must replace, and the 'Skills' tab hands you `npx skills add Jakubantalik/transitions.dev`, a third-party skill for a different library, not an Amicro one. The npm package has only two published versions (July 2026), so pin the version.
why_it_matters: The dither-shaded chart set is a genuinely uncommon aesthetic delivered as installable React source, which is rarer than another Tailwind button pack.
notable_for: no static docs — hash-routed SPA only
evidence: https://amicro.vercel.app/ (raw HTML — JS shell), https://amicro.vercel.app/assets/index-Q0a5OWJD.js (bundle, component ids extracted), https://amicro.vercel.app/sitemap.xml, https://amicro.vercel.app/components (404), https://api.github.com/repos/Subhan-code/Amicro--Micro-transitions-, https://registry.npmjs.org/@subhanhq/amicro

name: NumberFlow
tagline: Dependency-free animated number component for React, Vue, Svelte and JS
description: NumberFlow by Maxwell Barvian animates a number as its value changes, rendering an odometer-style digit roll. It is built on a custom element with no runtime dependencies and ships as four MIT packages — @number-flow/react, @number-flow/vue, @number-flow/svelte and the framework-agnostic number-flow. Formatting goes through Intl.NumberFormatOptions so currency, percent, compact notation and locale come free; transform, spin and opacity timings are independently controllable, digit trend can be forced up, down or neutral, and prefers-reduced-motion is respected. Styling is done through CSS ::part selectors and custom properties, NumberFlowGroup syncs several instances whose layout shifts affect each other, and a `continuous` plugin makes a transition appear to pass through the intermediate numbers.
agent_guidance: Reach for NumberFlow any time a displayed number changes and the change should be legible — pricing toggles, live counters, stat tiles, cart totals, usage meters — instead of hand-rolling a count-up with a spring library. It composes with anything because the core is a custom element with zero dependencies: install @number-flow/react, @number-flow/vue or @number-flow/svelte to match the host app, and use the plain `number-flow` package outside a framework. Two gotchas: pass formatting through the `format` prop as Intl.NumberFormatOptions rather than pre-formatting the string, or the digit diffing breaks; and wrap instances in NumberFlowGroup when one animating number shifts another's position, otherwise their transitions desync.
why_it_matters: The reference implementation for animated numbers on the web — four framework bindings, no dependencies, motion-preference aware, and 7.6k stars behind it. There is no reason to write this yourself.
notable_for: React, Vue, Svelte and vanilla packages

name: FIFA World Cup 26 IP Guidelines
tagline: 28-page FIFA PDF cataloguing the World Cup 26 marks and their permitted use
description: The official FIFA Intellectual Property Guidelines for the FIFA World Cup 26, version 2.0, dated June 2024, in eight sections across 28 pages. Section 2 inventories the protected assets: the Official Emblem (trophy set inside a stacked 2/6), the Official Wordmark, the Official Slogan lockups 'WE ARE 26' / 'SOMOS 26' / 'NOUS SOMMES 26' in single-line and stacked forms, the 16 Host City logos in their per-city colourways and patterns, Host City slogan lockups, the trophy, the FIFA corporate mark, the FIFA Plus mark, a list of registered word marks, and the bespoke Official Typeface 'FWC 26'. Sections 3 to 6 explain the rights-holder tiers and media rules, and section 7 gives thirteen pages of worked examples of permitted and prohibited use. It is a legal usage document, not a visual identity manual — there are no colour values, grids or clear-space specifications.
agent_guidance: Treat this as a hard constraint document, not a source of assets: it is the authority on which World Cup 26 marks exist and it explicitly forbids non-rights-holders from any commercial use, so never generate, trace or approximate the emblem, the 'We Are 26' lockup, a Host City logo or the FWC 26 typeface into a deliverable. Consult section 7 (pages 14-26) when a client wants World Cup-adjacent creative — it draws the line between legitimate generic-football references and an unauthorised commercial association. Media outlets can request licensed artwork through fifadigitalarchive.com/welcome/markrequest; nothing here is downloadable as vectors.
why_it_matters: It is the primary-source record of the World Cup 26 identity system — every mark, every language variant, all 16 host-city colourways — from the rights holder itself, which is the correct citation when the identity is discussed or when a legal boundary must be respected.
notable_for: 13 pages of permitted vs prohibited use examples

name: World Cup 26 Logo Reaction
tagline: USA TODAY news piece on the World Cup 26 emblem launch and its backlash
description: A USA TODAY Sports report by Jordan Mendoza, syndicated to Yahoo Sports and dated 18 May 2023, covering FIFA's unveiling of the World Cup 26 identity at Griffith Observatory in Los Angeles. It records the design facts — the trophy used as a central element for the first time in World Cup branding, the vertically stacked '2' and '6', and 16 host-city variants with their own colours and local references such as Kansas City's 'City of Fountains' cue — alongside the 'We Are 26' campaign and Gianni Infantino's framing of it as three countries saying 'we are united as one'. The bulk of the piece is aggregated social-media reaction, which ran strongly negative: 'too basic', 'bland', and a comparison to 'Microsoft Paint in less than 5 minutes'. It is a reception record, not a design analysis.
agent_guidance: Cite this only as evidence of how the World Cup 26 identity landed with the public — it is a tweet round-up, so do not mine it for design rationale, colour values, or typographic detail. Pair it with the FIFA IP Guidelines PDF in this same batch, which is the primary source for what the marks actually are; this article is the reception half of that pair. If an argument needs a worked critique of a minimal sports identity, find a design-press analysis instead.
why_it_matters: A dated, quotable record that a deliberately reductive identity from a major rights holder drew immediate public backlash — useful ammunition when a stakeholder equates minimalism with safety.
notable_for: trophy in the emblem for the first time
reception record, aggregated from social media
